title: The Equalizing Power of Friendship
author: Jacob Allee
summary: Jacob Allee argues that friendship, defined as a bond formed by a common interest, commitment or love, is the great equalizer of the living. He tests the thesis against two pairs in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings. Sam and Frodo begin as servant and master, but shared labor and a shared commitment to destroying the Ring dissolve the distinction until Aragorn himself bows to them. Legolas and Gimli begin with seven millennia of inherited elf and dwarf distrust, and the turn comes when both love Galadriel and the beauty of Lothlorien. He then extends the claim to the Christian Scriptures, where Christ calls disciples friends rather than servants and abolishes the divisions between Jew and Gentile. The essay is a Great Books style reading that treats literature as evidence for a claim about what forms human community.
points: Allee defines friendship as two people standing side by side looking at something shared, following C. S. Lewis, which explains why a common object of love can erase rank.
The Frodo and Sam example shows inequality shrinking through shared hardship and a common mission rather than through any deliberate leveling.
The Legolas and Gimli example shows that inherited, mythic prejudice can be overcome when two people admire the same good thing.
The essay models a classical way of reading, using close attention to scenes from a canonical story to support a general thesis about human relations.
The biblical section reframes friendship with Christ as the root of equality between believers, which is the author's deepest layer of the argument.
quotes: Friendship is the term we use to describe the bond between two or more people which is, or has been, formed by a common interest, commitment, or love. C. S. Lewis once described the difference between romantic love and friendship as the difference between two people looking directly at one another as opposed to standing side by side looking at something else.
Their common commitment to the destruction of the One Ring and, more to the point, the preservation of the Shire, all but eliminates any real or meaningful distinctions of inequality between them.

The humility of Sam, ever evident, struggles to see what Frodo sees and what the reader sees, that these two hobbits are no longer servant and master, not really, they are friends who would each lay down his life for the other without a second thought.

It is these and many other such stories throughout the history of Middle Earth which add up to about 7,000 years of bad blood between elves and dwarves, and all of that hangs in the air between Gimli and Legolas when they are put into each other’s company to become part of the Fellowship of the Ring.

This moment marks a definite turn in their relationship, a turn towards friendship, a turn towards equality in one another’s sight, and it comes by a mutual love and affection for the beauty and goodness of Galadriel and the wondrousness of Lothlórien itself.

Every person who has ever had a true friend knows the equalizing power of friendship. Friendship makes bosses and employees forget their relative positions as they cheer on their same beloved sports team.

The more people focus their admiration upon something not themselves, the more they unite in a common purpose to accomplish something important, the more they forget themselves and look to the other, the more they become equal because the other takes precedence.
